facts.title: Named For Being Hard To Get
facts.text: Dysprosium's name comes from the Greek word "dysprositos," meaning "hard to obtain." French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran first separated it in 1886 in Paris, but only after performing more than 30 painstaking cycles of precipitation. The element's very name is an honest confession of how stubbornly it resisted isolation.

facts.title: Decades To Become Pure
facts.text: Although discovered in 1886, dysprosium could not be obtained in a reasonably pure form until the development of ion-exchange and solvent-extraction techniques in the 1950s. Frank Spedding and colleagues at Iowa State University pioneered these separation methods. Only then could chemists finally study the metal's true properties rather than working with rare-earth mixtures.

facts.title: A Champion Of Magnetism
facts.text: Dysprosium has one of the highest magnetic moments of any element, with each atom carrying up to 10 Bohr magnetons from its unpaired 4f electrons. Below about 85 kelvin it becomes ferromagnetic, and it holds the highest known magnetic strength among elements at very low temperatures. This is why it is prized for high-performance magnets.

facts.title: The Heat-Proofing Additive
facts.text: Adding a few percent of dysprosium to neodymium-iron-boron magnets dramatically raises their resistance to demagnetization at high temperatures. This makes Dy essential in the powerful magnets inside electric-vehicle motors and wind-turbine generators, which can run hot. Without dysprosium, these magnets would lose their strength in demanding industrial conditions.

facts.title: A Critical Raw Material
facts.text: Dysprosium is classified as a critical raw material by the European Union and the United States because supply is scarce and concentrated. More than 90 percent of the world's heavy rare earths, including dysprosium, are produced in China. Its strategic importance for green-energy technology makes securing new sources a global priority.

facts.title: Soaking Up Neutrons
facts.text: Dysprosium absorbs neutrons extremely well, which makes it valuable in nuclear reactor control rods. Cermets of dysprosium oxide mixed with nickel are used to regulate the chain reaction, and the material resists swelling and corrosion under intense radiation. This combination of neutron appetite and durability is unusually good for reactor service.

facts.title: It Glows Under Stress
facts.text: When activated with impurities, dysprosium compounds are phosphors that emit light. Dysprosium-doped calcium sulfate and calcium fluoride are used as dosimeters, glowing when heated after exposure to ionizing radiation in a process called thermoluminescence. Workers in nuclear and medical fields wear such badges to measure the radiation dose they have received.

facts.title: A Crystal That Changes Shape
facts.text: In the alloy Terfenol-D, dysprosium teams up with terbium and iron to produce one of the strongest known magnetostrictive effects. The material physically changes its length when placed in a magnetic field, expanding or contracting by a tiny but useful amount. This property powers precise actuators, sonar transducers, and ultrasonic devices.

facts.title: No Job In Living Things
facts.text: Dysprosium has no known biological role in any organism, and humans contain only trace amounts absorbed from the environment. It is generally considered to have low toxicity, with soluble salts being only mildly hazardous. Because cells never evolved to use it, the body simply has no machinery that depends on this metal.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: Dysprosium is built in the cosmos mainly through rapid neutron capture, the r-process, during catastrophic events such as merging neutron stars and certain supernovae. On Earth it never occurs as a free metal but is found in minerals like xenotime and monazite. Its presence in the crust is a fingerprint of violent nuclear furnaces that existed long before our solar system formed.
